opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think Chinchilla is a really important paper, but it's often misread. What Chinchilla tells you is: given a fixed compute budget for *training*, what's the optimal split between model size and number of tokens to get the best loss at the end of training. That's a great answer to the question "how do I train the best model for a paper or a research comparison with fixed FLOPs." But it's not really the question you're asking when you're building a model that millions of people are going to use.

When you think about deployment, the cost that dominates isn't training anymore, it's inference. Every single query someone sends goes through the model, and that cost scales with the number of parameters. So if you take the Chinchilla-optimal point, you end up with a model that's quite large for its quality, and it's expensive to serve forever. Whereas if you take a smaller model and just keep training it on way more tokens than Chinchilla would recommend, you pay more at training time, sometimes much more than "optimal," but you get a model that's cheaper and faster at inference and still very strong.

And what we saw empirically is that the models don't really saturate as fast as people expected. You keep feeding tokens, well past the Chinchilla ratio of roughly twenty tokens per parameter, and the loss keeps going down. Slowly, but it keeps going down. So for something like the 7B models, training on a trillion tokens or two trillion tokens, which is wildly "over-trained" by Chinchilla standards, is actually the right decision if your goal is a model that the community can run on a single GPU, fine-tune, and build on.

So the way I think about it is: you have to fold the inference budget into the equation. Total cost is training compute plus the expected usage times the per-token inference cost. Once you do that, the optimum shifts quite dramatically toward smaller models trained for much longer. Chinchilla is still useful as a reference point, it tells you where you're being compute-inefficient during training, but it's not the target. The target is the best model at a given inference size, and that's a different optimization problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Chinchilla is a great paper, but I think people often misread what it's actually optimizing. The question Chinchilla answers is: given a fixed training compute budget, what's the best trade-off between parameters and tokens to minimize training loss? And the answer was roughly twenty tokens per parameter. That's the right answer to that question. But it's not the question you care about when you're going to deploy a model.

When you deploy, the cost is dominated by inference, not training. You train once, and then you serve billions of queries. So the real objective is not to minimize the training loss for a given training compute, it's to minimize the total cost, training plus inference, for a given level of quality. And once you include inference in the equation, the optimum shifts dramatically toward smaller models trained on far more tokens. A smaller model is cheaper to serve, has lower latency, fits on fewer GPUs, and people can actually run it.

That's really what we did with Llama. With Llama 2, the 7B model was trained on two trillion tokens, which is way beyond what Chinchilla would call optimal, something like fifteen times more. And with Llama 3 we went to fifteen trillion tokens, even for the 8B. From a pure Chinchilla perspective, that's "wasting" compute. But what we observed is that the loss keeps going down, log-linearly, and the model keeps improving on downstream tasks. We didn't see saturation. So you pay more at training time, once, and you get a model that is much better for its size at inference time, forever.

The other thing I would say is that Chinchilla's scaling laws are about loss, and loss is a proxy. What matters is the capability at the end, and we've seen that you can sometimes get more by keeping training a smaller model than by scaling the parameters, especially once you factor in post-training. A strong small model is also just more useful to the community: researchers can fine-tune it, people can run it locally. So in practice, I think about Chinchilla as a lower bound on how many tokens you should use, not a target. If you're building a model for people to use, you should almost always overtrain it relative to the Chinchilla optimum, and the only real constraint is how much high-quality data you can get and how much training compute you're willing to spend up front.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is that Chinchilla tells you how to allocate compute if you want the best model for a fixed training budget. But when you deploy a model, training is only one part of the cost. You also have to account for inference, and that cost grows every time someone uses it.

So you might prefer to train a smaller model for much longer than the Chinchilla-optimal point. You spend more upfront, but you get a model that is cheaper to serve on every request. If you have enough usage, that tradeoff makes a lot of sense.

The question becomes: what quality do you need, and how much inference do you expect? There isn’t one optimal model size independent of those assumptions. Chinchilla is a useful starting point, but the training-optimal choice isn’t necessarily the deployment-optimal choice.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is that Chinchilla gives you an optimal allocation of compute for training. But if you’re building a model that people will use a lot, you care about the cost of inference as well.

So you might prefer to train a smaller model for much longer than the Chinchilla-optimal number of tokens. You spend more upfront, but then every inference is cheaper. If you serve enough requests, that trade-off makes sense.

There isn’t one optimal model size independently of how you’re going to use it. You have to consider the training budget, the expected volume of inference, and the quality and latency you need. Chinchilla is a useful starting point, but it doesn’t by itself give you the optimal model to deploy.
